opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is the environment, and the feedback the agent gets from it, more than any single model trick.

When people talk about agents, they often focus on the model: bigger, smarter, better reasoning. That matters, of course. But for tasks that are really broad and open-ended, the bottleneck is usually whether the agent can interact with a rich, realistic environment and learn from what happens. Can it try something, see the result, notice it was wrong, and correct itself? That loop is what turns a model that can talk into one that can actually get things done.

So for me there are a few layers.

First, the base model has to be strong in a general way, not just good at benchmarks. It needs solid reasoning, real coding ability, and a good sense of when it doesn't know something. Coding is especially important because so much agent work eventually becomes "write a bit of code, run it, check the output."

Second is the environment and the reward. If you want generalization, you can't train on a handful of narrow, hand-crafted tasks. You need diverse, verifiable tasks where the signal is honest. If the reward can be gamed, the model will game it, and you end up with something that looks impressive in evaluation but falls apart in real use. A lot of the unglamorous work is building environments and verifiers you can trust.

Third is long-horizon robustness. Real tasks aren't five steps. They're fifty or a hundred, with tool failures, ambiguous instructions, and information you have to go find. An agent that's 95% reliable per step is useless over a long task. So consistency, recovering from errors, and managing context over long trajectories matter much more than peak cleverness on any single step.

And finally, honestly, taste: deciding which problems are worth solving. With limited compute and people, you have to bet on what will generalize, instead of chasing whatever looks good on a leaderboard this month.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: a strong general model, trained through honest feedback from diverse, realistic environments, with a lot of attention on reliability over long tasks. That's what makes an agent broadly useful rather than just a good demo.

r001.rationale: The candidate emphasizes general reasoning, coding, environments, feedback, and long-horizon reliability, but does not identify multimodal understanding as especially important.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention tenfold cost savings or any cost-based adoption threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about agents for broadly applicable tasks, the thing I keep coming back to is that the hardest part isn't getting the model to do one thing well. It's getting it to do many things reliably, in environments it has never seen, with tools it wasn't specifically trained on.

So I'd say three things matter most.

The first is generalization over specialization. It's very tempting to build a great coding agent, or a great browsing agent, by stacking task-specific scaffolding on top of the model. That works for demos. But every piece of hand-written scaffolding is a place where the agent breaks when the task shifts slightly. What we really want is for the capability to live in the model itself: the ability to read a new environment, understand what tools are available, plan, and recover from mistakes. If the model has that, the scaffolding can be thin, and thin scaffolding is what transfers.

The second is long-horizon reliability. A single-turn model can be right ninety percent of the time and feel excellent. An agent that takes fifty steps, each ninety percent reliable, almost never finishes. So the question shifts from "how smart is the model" to "how well does it notice when it's wrong, and how well does it correct course." Self-verification, checking intermediate results, knowing when to ask instead of guessing. Those are learned behaviors, and you have to train for them deliberately, mostly through reinforcement learning in realistic environments rather than through imitation of clean trajectories.

The third, and people underestimate this, is the environment and the feedback signal. Whatever you optimize for, the agent will become. If your reward is "the task passed some test," the agent learns to pass tests, which is not quite the same as solving the problem. Building environments that are diverse, that are hard to game, and where the reward actually reflects what a human would consider good work is probably the most important and least glamorous part of the whole thing. It's where most of the real effort goes.

And underneath all of that, you still need a strong base model. There's no amount of agent training that fixes a model that doesn't understand the world well. So it's base capability, then teaching the model to act and verify over long horizons, then being extremely careful about what you're actually rewarding. Get those right and the agent generalizes. Get them wrong and you have something that looks impressive on a benchmark and falls apart the first time a user asks it something slightly different.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization across unfamiliar environments and tools, but does not identify multimodal understanding as especially important.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention cost savings or a roughly tenfold threshold for adopting an AI agent.

astra-6.text:
I think what matters most is whether an agent can adapt when the task changes. For broadly applicable tasks, you can’t anticipate every situation and write a workflow for it. The model needs to understand the goal, identify what information is missing, choose useful tools, and adjust when the results don’t match its expectations.

That makes the feedback loop especially important. Taking an action is only one part of the process; the agent also needs to judge whether that action helped. Can it recognize a mistake, recover from it, and know when to ask the user for clarification?

So I would focus on strong underlying capabilities and evaluation across varied, realistic tasks. A successful demonstration is encouraging, but the more important question is whether the agent remains reliable when the instructions are ambiguous or something unexpected happens.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes adaptability, feedback, and evaluation, but does not identify multimodal understanding as especially important.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention roughly tenfold cost savings or a cost threshold for adopting an AI agent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what matters most is whether an agent can learn to handle situations we didn’t explicitly design for. You can build a system that performs well on a carefully defined workflow, but broadly applicable tasks require it to understand a goal, identify what information is missing, choose useful tools, and adjust when something goes wrong.

That makes the feedback loop very important. The agent needs a way to check whether its actions actually moved it closer to the goal. Producing a plausible answer isn’t enough—if it writes code, does the code work? If it gathers information, does that information support the conclusion?

I would also emphasize knowing when to ask for help. A useful agent should act independently when it has enough information, but recognize uncertainty and involve the user when a decision needs their judgment. General capability has to come with that kind of reliability.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes adapting to unfamiliar situations, feedback, and reliability, but does not identify multimodal understanding as especially important.

r002.rationale: The response gives no cost-savings threshold or adoption criterion.
